title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXVI
paragraphs:
He beats me and I rail at him: O worthy satisfaction! would it were
otherwise—that I could beat him while he railed at me.—_Troilus and
Cressida_.

Fred did not return to Stone Court the next day, for reasons that allowed no choice. His visits to Houndsley’s filthy streets in pursuit of Diamond had brought back more than a bad bargain in horseflesh. He had also caught an illness which for a day or two seemed merely low spirits and a headache. After his visit to Stone Court it grew so much worse that he went into the dining room and collapsed on the sofa. When his mother anxiously questioned him, he said, “I feel terribly ill. I think you’d better send for Wrench.”

Wrench came but suspected nothing serious. He described a “slight upset” and said nothing about returning the following day. He valued the Vincys’ custom properly, but even the most watchful men can be dulled by routine and, on harassed mornings, go through their duties with the enthusiasm of someone ringing the same bell every day. Mr. Wrench was a small, neat, bilious man with a carefully dressed wig, a demanding practice, an irritable temper, a sluggish wife, and seven children. He was already late for a four-mile drive to meet Dr. Minchin beyond Tipton. Hicks, a country practitioner, had died, increasing business for Middlemarch doctors in that direction. Great statesmen make mistakes; why shouldn’t small medical men? Wrench did not forget to send the usual white packets, which this time contained dark, powerful purgatives. They brought poor Fred no relief. Still unwilling, as he said, to believe he was “in for an illness,” he got up at his usual leisurely hour the next morning and came down intending to eat breakfast. Instead he could do nothing but sit shivering by the fire. They sent for Wrench again, but he was out on his rounds. Seeing her darling’s altered face and general misery, Mrs. Vincy began to cry and said she would call Dr. Sprague.
“Don’t be silly, mother. It’s nothing,” said Fred, reaching his hot, dry hand towards her. “I’ll soon be well. I must have caught cold on that horrible wet ride.”

“Mamma!” said Rosamond, sitting near the window. The dining room overlooked the highly respectable street called Lowick Gate. “There’s Mr. Lydgate, stopping to talk to someone. I’d call him in if I were you. He cured Ellen Bulstrode. People say he cures everyone.”

Mrs. Vincy sprang to the window and threw it open, thinking only of Fred and nothing of medical etiquette. Lydgate stood only two yards away beyond the iron railings. He turned at the sudden sound of the sash before she called. Within two minutes he was in the room. Rosamond withdrew after waiting just long enough to show a pretty anxiety struggling with her sense of propriety.

Lydgate listened to an account in which Mrs. Vincy’s mind instinctively fastened on every minor detail, especially what Wrench had and had not said about returning. He immediately saw that trouble with Wrench might follow, but the seriousness of the case put that consideration aside. He was convinced Fred had reached the pink-spotted stage of typhoid fever and had received exactly the wrong medicines. He must go straight to bed, have a regular nurse, and be given various treatments and precautions about which Lydgate was precise. These signs of danger terrified Mrs. Vincy, whose fear poured out in whatever words came easiest. It was “very bad treatment from Mr. Wrench, whom they’d employed for so many years instead of Mr. Peacock, though Peacock was just as much a friend. Why should Wrench neglect her children more than anyone else’s? She couldn’t understand it. He hadn’t neglected Mrs. Larcher’s children when they had measles, nor would Mrs. Vincy have wanted him to. And if anything happened—”

Here she broke down completely, her beautiful throat and good-natured face painfully convulsed. They were in the hall, beyond Fred’s hearing, but Rosamond had opened the drawing-room door and now approached anxiously. Lydgate defended Wrench. Yesterday’s symptoms might have been misleading; this kind of fever was very uncertain at first. He would go immediately to the chemist and have a prescription prepared to avoid delay, then write to Wrench explaining what had been done.

“But you must come back. You must keep treating Fred. I can’t leave my boy to someone who may come or may not. Thank God I bear nobody ill will, and Mr. Wrench saved me when I had pleurisy. But he’d better have let me die if—if—”
“Shall I meet Mr. Wrench here, then?” Lydgate asked, genuinely believing Wrench ill-equipped to handle such a case wisely.
“Please arrange it, Mr. Lydgate,” said Rosamond, coming to her mother’s help and supporting her arm to lead her away.

When Mr. Vincy came home he was furious with Wrench and did not care if he ever entered the house again. Lydgate would continue, whether Wrench liked it or not. Fever in the house was no joke. Everyone must be told not to come to Thursday’s dinner. Pritchard need not bring up wine; brandy was best against infection. “I shall drink brandy,” Mr. Vincy declared emphatically, as though this were no time for blank cartridges. “Fred’s an extraordinarily unlucky boy. He’ll need a good turn of luck later to make up for this. Otherwise I don’t know who’d want an eldest son.”
“Don’t say that, Vincy,” his wife said, her lip trembling, “unless you want him taken from me.”

“The worry will kill you, Lucy. I can see that,” he said more gently. “Still, Wrench shall hear what I think.” His confused feeling was that proper concern for his family—the Mayor’s family—might somehow have prevented the fever. “I’m the last man to join the fuss about new doctors, or new parsons either, whether they’re Bulstrode’s men or not. But Wrench shall hear my opinion, however he takes it.”

Wrench took it badly. Lydgate was as polite as his casual manner allowed, but politeness from someone who has put you at a disadvantage only makes matters worse, especially if you disliked him already. Country practitioners used to be an irritable breed, touchy about their honor, and Wrench ranked among the most irritable. He agreed to meet Lydgate that evening, but the occasion tried his temper. He had to hear Mrs. Vincy exclaim:
“Oh, Mr. Wrench, what have I done to deserve this? Going away and never coming back! My boy might have been lying dead!”
Mr. Vincy had kept up a brisk attack on the enemy Infection and was considerably heated by it. Hearing Wrench arrive, he jumped up and went into the hall to deliver his opinion.

“I’ll tell you, Wrench, this is beyond a joke,” said the Mayor. Lately accustomed to rebuking offenders in an official manner, he now made himself broader by hooking his thumbs into his waistcoat armholes. “Letting fever steal into a house like this! Some things ought to be grounds for a lawsuit and aren’t. That’s my opinion.”

Yet unreasonable accusations were easier to bear than being taught, or rather sensing that a younger man like Lydgate privately thought he needed teaching. For “the fact was,” Wrench later said, Lydgate paraded fanciful foreign ideas that would not last. He swallowed his anger for the moment but afterwards wrote declining further attendance. The household might be valuable, but he would not bow to anyone over a professional matter. With considerable probability on his side, he reflected that sooner or later Lydgate would make a mistake too. His ungentlemanly attacks on other practitioners’ sale of medicines would eventually rebound upon him. Wrench made cutting remarks about Lydgate’s tricks, worthy only of a quack, for building an artificial reputation among gullible people. Sound practitioners never stirred up that kind of cant about cures.

On this point Lydgate was as sore as Wrench could wish. Promotion by ignorant admirers was not merely humiliating but dangerous, no more enviable than a weather prophet’s reputation. The foolish expectations surrounding every kind of work made him impatient. His unprofessional frankness could easily harm him as much as Wrench hoped.

Nevertheless, Lydgate became the Vincys’ doctor, and Middlemarch discussed the event widely. Some said the family had behaved disgracefully: Vincy had threatened Wrench, and Mrs. Vincy had accused him of poisoning her son. Others thought Lydgate’s passing had been providential, that he was exceptionally skilled with fevers, and that Bulstrode was right to promote him. Many believed Bulstrode had been responsible for his coming to town at all. Mrs. Taft, always counting stitches and collecting information in misleading fragments between rows of knitting, had acquired the notion that Lydgate was Bulstrode’s illegitimate son. This seemed to confirm her suspicions about Evangelical laymen.
One day she passed this information to Mrs. Farebrother, who duly told her son, remarking:
“Nothing about Bulstrode would surprise me, but I’d be sorry to believe it of Mr. Lydgate.”
After a burst of laughter, Mr. Farebrother replied, “Mother, you know perfectly well that Lydgate comes from a good northern family. He’d never heard of Bulstrode before arriving here.”
“That’s satisfactory as far as Mr. Lydgate is concerned, Camden,” the old lady said with an air of exactness. “But as for Bulstrode, the report may be true about some other son.”
